title: A Tearful Letter, a Forgiven Offender, and the Aroma of Christ
summary: Paul explains why he did not make another painful visit to Corinth and instead wrote a letter "through many tears". He urges the church to forgive and comfort a man they have disciplined, so that Satan will not gain an advantage. Then he recalls his restless search for Titus in Troas and Macedonia, and breaks into thanks to God, who leads his apostles in Christ's triumphal procession and spreads through them the fragrance of the knowledge of Christ.
story: Second Corinthians is the letter of a strained relationship being mended. After founding the church in Corinth (Acts 18), Paul wrote at least one letter before 1 Corinthians (1 Corinthians 5:9), then 1 Corinthians itself, and then things went badly. Chapter 1 has explained why he changed his travel plans; chapter 2 continues that explanation and reveals more of what happened: a "painful visit", a letter written in anguish, and an offender who wronged Paul or the church. The chapter then opens the long reflection on apostolic ministry that runs from 2:14 to 7:4, before Paul returns to the story of Titus's arrival in 7:5.
historical:
The events behind this chapter have to be pieced together from the letter itself. Paul had evidently made a second visit to Corinth, not recorded in Acts, which he calls painful (verse 1; compare 12:14 and 13:1-2, where he speaks of coming a third time). Instead of another such visit he wrote a letter "out of great distress and anguish of heart" (verse 4), often called the tearful or severe letter. Scholars differ on what it was. Some identify it with 1 Corinthians, but 1 Corinthians does not read like a letter written through tears, so most think it is a letter now lost. Others think chapters 10-13 of 2 Corinthians preserve part of it.

The offender of verses 5-11 is also debated. Older interpreters often identified him with the man living with his father's wife in 1 Corinthians 5. Many modern scholars think instead of someone who publicly opposed or insulted Paul during the painful visit, since Paul speaks of the harm as done to the church and, in a qualified way, to himself. Either way, the church had disciplined him by majority decision, and Paul now judges it enough. Troas, where Paul found an open door for the gospel, was a port on the northwest coast of Asia Minor, the usual crossing point to Macedonia in northern Greece (Acts 16:8-11). Titus, a Gentile coworker (Galatians 2:3), had carried Paul's message to Corinth, and Paul was anxious to hear how it had been received.
cultural:
Paul's image in verse 14 comes from the Roman triumph, the victory parade granted to a conquering general. The general rode through Rome in a chariot, preceded by spoils and by prisoners of war, some of whom would be executed at the end. The verb thriambeuo means to lead in such a procession, and the BSB renders it "leads us triumphantly as captives". Paul pictures himself not as the victor but as one of Christ's conquered captives, put on display. Some scholars think the aroma of verses 14-16 continues the picture, since incense and spices were burned along a triumphal route, and that the same smell meant life to the victors and death to the captives. Others hear an echo of the sacrifices of the Old Testament, which rose as a pleasing aroma to God. Both backgrounds fit the text.

The word "peddle" in verse 17 translates a verb used of petty traders, especially wine sellers, who had a reputation for watering down their goods and haggling for profit. Travelling speakers who charged for their teaching were common in the Greek cities, and some of Paul's rivals in Corinth seem to have accepted payment. Paul, who worked with his hands to support himself in Corinth (Acts 18:3; 1 Corinthians 9:12-18), refuses to treat the gospel as merchandise.
literary: The chapter falls into three movements. Verses 1-4 continue Paul's defense of his changed plans with the vocabulary of grief and joy, repeated again and again: grieve, sorrow, rejoice, tears, love. Verses 5-11 turn the same emotional language toward the offender, with the goal of forgiveness and restoration. Verses 12-13 begin a travel narrative, and then, abruptly, verse 14 turns to thanksgiving. The travel story does not resume until 7:5, where the next words about Macedonia pick up exactly where 2:13 left off. Some scholars take the break as evidence that separate letters have been joined; others see a deliberate digression in which the mention of Titus leads Paul into a long reflection on what ministry is. Verse 16 ends with a question, "And who is qualified for such a task?", which chapter 3 answers.

outline.t: Why Paul wrote instead of coming
No rest in Troas without Titus
Led in Christ's triumph, spreading his fragrance

doctrines.note: Church discipline in this chapter has a goal beyond punishment: the restoration of the offender. The church acts together ("by the majority"), and when discipline has done its work, the same body must forgive, comfort, and reaffirm its love, so that the person is not overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.

Paul assumes the offender has turned, and he calls the church to match repentance with forgiveness. Withholding forgiveness from the repentant is not strictness but a foothold for Satan, whose schemes include turning a community's grief into bitterness or despair.

The apostles spread "the fragrance of the knowledge of Him" everywhere. The same message divides its hearers, bringing life to some and death to others, and so Paul insists it must be spoken with sincerity, never sold for profit.

words.note: Lupe, grief or sorrow. With its verb it runs through verses 1-7 more often than in almost any other passage of Paul. It covers pain inflicted and pain felt, and Paul uses it to show that his severe letter came from love, not anger. Chapter 7 will distinguish godly sorrow, which leads to repentance, from worldly sorrow.

Charizomai, to forgive, literally to give freely or show grace; it shares a root with charis, grace. Forgiveness here is a gracious gift, not a grudging concession. Paul uses the word four times in verses 7-10, and he says he has forgiven "in the presence of Christ", the one whose grace underlies all theirs.

Thriambeuo, to lead in a triumphal procession. The word comes from the Roman victory parade. Its exact force here is debated, whether God leads the apostles as captives displayed in Christ's victory or as participants in it, but the image of defeat turned into God's victory prepares for Paul's theme of strength in weakness.

Kapeleuo, to peddle, to trade in something for gain, with overtones of adulterating the goods. It appears only here in the New Testament. Paul contrasts it with speaking "with sincerity, as men sent from God".

christ: Christ stands at the center of each part of the chapter. Paul forgives "in the presence of Christ" (verse 10), and forgiveness in the church mirrors the forgiveness Christ has given. The gospel Paul carries to Troas is "the gospel of Christ" (verse 12). And in the triumph image of verse 14 it is Christ, not Paul, who is the conqueror; the apostles are the captives in his procession, and through them God spreads the knowledge of him. Believers themselves become "the sweet aroma of Christ" before God (verse 15). The paradox that a parade of the defeated displays a victory anticipates the letter's claim that God's power is shown in the weakness of his servants, as it was in the weakness of the cross (13:4).
questions: Paul urges the church to forgive a man they have disciplined so that he is not overwhelmed by excessive sorrow. Why do communities, and individuals, find it hard to end a punishment once it has done its work?
Paul had an open door for the gospel in Troas but no peace in his spirit, and he left. What does this honest detail say about the emotional life of a faithful servant of God?
The same message is a fragrance of life to some and an odor of death to others. How have you seen the gospel divide people who heard the same words?
